title: Do Your Students Know You're In Charge?
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin describes three telltale signs that students have filled a leadership vacuum in a classroom: they offer unsolicited suggestions about how the teacher should run things, they become bold and disrespectful, and they develop a blase, disengaged attitude. He argues these behaviors stem directly from teachers who fail to clearly establish themselves as the classroom's ultimate authority, often by trying to be a buddy or facilitator instead. His solution is direct verbal reinforcement - literally telling students, repeatedly and with conviction, that the teacher is in charge and responsible for every decision - backed by a real classroom management plan. He closes by reframing disrespectful behavior as a response to uninspired leadership rather than defiance for its own sake, suggesting students actually want a strong leader to follow.
points: Three warning signs of a classroom leadership vacuum: unsolicited suggestions, bold disrespect, and a blase attitude.
Trying to be a facilitator or buddy rather than the clear authority invites students to exploit the gap.
Teachers must explicitly and repeatedly tell students they are in charge, not just assume it is understood.
Words of authority must be backed by real conviction and a functioning classroom management plan.
Disengaged or defiant behavior often reflects a lack of inspiring leadership rather than pure misbehavior.
quotes: There is a lot that stands out in your mind while teaching students from both ends of the classroom management spectrum. But one thing is indisputable. In classrooms with poor classroom management, the students believe they are, to some degree, in charge.
When a teacher leaves a leadership vacuum of any kind, and to any degree, the students will fill it with a vengeance.

Your students may not yet be able to write a coherent paragraph, read at grade level, or tie their shoes, but if they’re unsure about who the ultimate authority in the classroom is, they’ll tell you how you should do your job.
Absent of strong leadership, there is no sense of urgency in students, no bright-eyed enthusiasm, and little work ethic.
The fact is, when a teacher reveals him or herself as less than the ultimate authority in the classroom, the students will exploit it for all it’s worth.
I’m your teacher and I’m in charge of this classroom. That’s my job. That means I make the decisions. I decide how you behave, what we learn, how we learn, and when we do the things we do.
Deep down our students don’t want to slouch or goof off or tell us how to do our jobs. They do it because they’re uninspired.
